questions.enonce_markdown: What is the converse of 'All beautiful housewives are university lecturers' ?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The given proposition is an **A** proposition ("All S are P", with S = beautiful housewives and P = university lecturers). Conversion means interchanging the subject and the predicate while keeping the quality (affirmative) unchanged. Because in an A proposition only the subject is distributed, a *simple* conversion ("All P are S", option D) would distribute the term S in the converse without having been distributed in the original, which is illegitimate (a counter-model: all squares are rectangles, but not all rectangles are squares). The A proposition is therefore converted *by limitation* (per accidens): "All S are P" gives "Some P are S", that is **Some university lecturers are beautiful housewives**. Option B changes the quality (it is an E proposition), and option C is the subaltern of the original ("Some S are P"), not its converse. Note: conversion by limitation, like the subaltern inference, presupposes that the subject class is not empty (existential import of traditional logic).

**Answer: A.**

choix.texte: Some university lecturers are beautiful housewives .
No university lecturers are beautiful housewives.
All university lecturers are beautiful housewives.

questions.enonce_markdown: The 'Opposition' in which the propositions differ in quantity and quality is :
questions.corrige_markdown:
In the traditional Square of Opposition, the four forms of opposition are distinguished by what the two propositions share: **contraries** (A and E) have the same quantity (both universal) but differ in quality; **subcontraries** (I and O) have the same quantity (both particular) but differ in quality; **subalternation** (A and I, E and O) concerns propositions with the same quality but different quantity; **contradictories** (A and O, E and I) differ in BOTH quantity and quality. The opposition asked for is therefore contradiction.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Which Fallacy is most clearly committed in this Syllogism ?

All musicians are dancers.
No drummers are musicians.
Therefore No drummers are dancers.
questions.corrige_markdown:
Identify the terms: major term P = dancers, minor term S = drummers, middle term M = musicians. The syllogism is: All M are P (A), No S are M (E), therefore No S are P (E), that is the mood AEE in the first figure. **Distribution:** the conclusion is negative, so its predicate P (dancers) is distributed. In the major premise "All musicians are dancers" the term "dancers" is the predicate of an A proposition and is NOT distributed. A term distributed in the conclusion but not in its premise is an **illicit process of the major term: Illicit Major**. The minor term is fine (S is distributed in the E premise, so distributing it in the conclusion is legitimate) and the middle term is distributed in the A premise, so there is no undistributed middle. Invalidity check (done with Python): take M = {1}, P = {1, 2}, S = {2}; both premises are true (M is included in P, S and M share no member) but "No S are P" is false since 2 is in both S and P. (The minor premise is also negative, which breaks the special rule of the first figure; the fallacy named by the question is the Illicit Major. "Illicit process" is only the generic name of the Illicit Major and the Illicit Minor.)

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: What precisely determines the First Order Enthymeme of a valid syllogism ?
questions.corrige_markdown:
An enthymeme is a syllogism stated with one of its three propositions suppressed (understood but not expressed). The traditional classification is by what is left out: in the **first order enthymeme the major premise is omitted** ("Socrates is a man, therefore he is mortal"), in the **second order enthymeme the minor premise is omitted** ("All men are mortal, therefore Socrates is mortal"), and in the **third order enthymeme the conclusion is omitted**. Option B is only the general definition of an enthymeme, not what *precisely* fixes the first order.

**Answer: D.**

choix.texte: When the minor premise is omitted.
When the major premise is omitted.

questions.enonce_markdown: A form of the Dilemma with a negative categorical conclusion is known as :
questions.corrige_markdown:
A dilemma is an argument with a conjunctive (two-conditional) major premise and a disjunctive minor premise. The four forms are:

| Form | Schema | Conclusion |
|---|---|---|
| Simple constructive | $(p \supset r) \cdot (q \supset r)$, $p \vee q$ | $r$ (affirmative categorical) |
| Complex constructive | $(p \supset r) \cdot (q \supset s)$, $p \vee q$ | $r \vee s$ (disjunctive) |
| Simple destructive | $(p \supset q) \cdot (p \supset r)$, $\sim q \vee \sim r$ | $\sim p$ (negative categorical) |
| Complex destructive | $(p \supset q) \cdot (r \supset s)$, $\sim q \vee \sim s$ | $\sim p \vee \sim r$ (disjunctive) |

(All four schemas were checked valid with a truth-table program.) The only form whose conclusion is a single negative proposition is the **Simple Destructive Dilemma**.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Given the following as a major premise :
' Either the rain falls or the sun shines' ,
construct a suitable minor premise for a valid Modus Ponendo Tollens,
questions.corrige_markdown:
*Modus Ponendo Tollens* ("the mode that, by affirming, denies") is the disjunctive syllogism whose minor premise AFFIRMS one alternative and whose conclusion DENIES the other: Either $p$ or $q$; $p$; therefore not $q$. It is valid only when the major premise is read as an exclusive disjunction ("either...or", not both); a program check shows it is invalid for the inclusive $p \vee q$ (counter-case: both true) and valid for the exclusive one. With the given major premise the suitable minor premise is **"The rain falls"**, from which follows "therefore the sun does not shine". Options B and C DENY an alternative: they belong to the *Modus Tollendo Ponens* (deny one, affirm the other). Option D contradicts the major premise, which would then be false.

**Answer: A.**
themes: rules of inference and argument forms

choix.texte: Neither did the rain fall nor did the sun shine.

questions.enonce_markdown: The Fallacy of 'affirming the consequent ' in a Modus Ponens argument is committed when:
questions.corrige_markdown:
The valid Modus Ponens is $p \supset q$, $p$, therefore $q$ (affirm the antecedent, conclude the consequent). The fallacy of *affirming the consequent* reverses the direction: $p \supset q$, $q$, therefore $p$, that is, **the minor premise affirms the consequent and the conclusion affirms the antecedent**. A truth-table check gives the counter-case $p$ false, $q$ true (both premises true, conclusion false). Option A is the valid Modus Tollens, option B is the fallacy of denying the antecedent, and option C is the valid Modus Ponens.

**Answer: D.**
themes: rules of inference and argument forms

choix.texte: The minor premise denies the consequent and conclusion the antecedent.
The minor premise denies the antecedent and conclusion the consequent.
The minor premise affirms the antecedent and conclusion the consequent.
The minor premise affirms the consequent and conclusion the antecedent.

questions.enonce_markdown: When a term in an argument is liable to more than one interpretation, it commits the Fallacy of :
questions.corrige_markdown:
The fallacies of ambiguity are of three kinds: **equivocation** (a *term* is used in two different senses in the same argument, e.g. "bank" as a river edge and as a financial institution), **amphiboly** (a *sentence* whose loose grammatical construction allows two readings) and **accent** (a shift of meaning through a change of emphasis or stress). A single TERM open to more than one interpretation gives equivocation. "Ambiguity" (option D) is the name of the whole family, not of the fallacy of a term.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A student who justifies his late coming on the basis that the teacher is always late also commits the Fallacy of :
questions.corrige_markdown:
*Tu quoque* ("you too") is a form of the argument against the person: one defends one's own conduct, or rejects a reproach, by pointing out that the accuser does the same thing. Here the student excuses his lateness by saying that the teacher is also always late; but the teacher's fault does not make the student's lateness right. *Ignoratio elenchi* is missing the point at issue, *ad populum* is an appeal to the feelings of the crowd and *non sequitur* is a conclusion that simply does not follow.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The statement : 'If Paul returns then Agnes will travel ' can best be symbolised as :
questions.corrige_markdown:
Let $p$ = "Paul returns" and $q$ = "Agnes will travel". "If ... then ..." is the conditional (material implication), written $p \supset q$. Option B is a disjunction ("or"), option C a conjunction ("and") and option D a conjunction with a negated first member.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Identify the form of the following argument ;

$p \supset q$
$\sim p$
$\therefore \sim q$
questions.corrige_markdown:
The premises are a conditional $p \supset q$ and the DENIAL of its antecedent $\sim p$; the conclusion denies the consequent. This is the fallacy of **denying the antecedent**. A truth table gives the counter-case $p$ false and $q$ true: both premises are true ($p \supset q$ is true because $p$ is false, $\sim p$ is true) and the conclusion $\sim q$ is false, so the form is invalid. The valid Modus Ponens affirms the antecedent ($p$, therefore $q$) and the valid Modus Tollens denies the consequent ($\sim q$, therefore $\sim p$); the given argument imitates the Modus Tollens with the wrong denial, so it is traditionally called an **invalid Modus Tollens**. "Modus Pollens" (option B) is a misprint of Ponens and is in any case not a valid form here.

**Answer: A.**
themes: rules of inference and argument forms

questions.enonce_markdown: Using quantification symbols of propositional functions the statement « none but thieves tell lies » can best be translated as :
questions.corrige_markdown:
Let $Tx$ = "x is a thief" and $Lx$ = "x tells lies". "None but thieves tell lies" is an exclusive proposition meaning "only thieves tell lies": whoever tells lies is a thief, equivalently "no non-thief tells lies". It is therefore the universal conditional with the liar as antecedent: $(x)(Lx \supset Tx)$. Checked by program on every interpretation over a three-member domain: only option A is equivalent to "no non-thief tells lies". Option B is the converse ("all thieves tell lies"), option C says that no liar is a thief, and option D says that no thief tells lies.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The quest for reasoned explanation for natural phenomena ushered the beginning of :
questions.corrige_markdown:
In the traditional account of the origins of Western thought, the Greek thinkers of Ionia (Thales and his successors) abandoned the mythological stories about gods in favour of explanations of nature by reason (*logos*) and observation. This turn from myth to reasoned inquiry into the nature and origin of things marks the **beginning of philosophy**. Mythology and religion explain by appeal to gods and revelation; the early natural philosophers explained by principles accessible to reason. (Science later grew out of this "natural philosophy", but in a philosophy syllabus the birth of rational inquiry is the birth of philosophy.)

**Answer: D.**
themes: myth and the origin of philosophy

questions.enonce_markdown: What is the distinct role that myths plays for a people ?
questions.corrige_markdown:
A myth is a traditional story, often about gods and the origin of things, that a people uses to explain the origin of the world, of humankind, of death and of the order of nature. What distinguishes myth from other cultural forms is precisely this explanatory role: it **provides answers to the fundamental questions about the people's existence** (where do we come from, why is there suffering and death, why does the world work as it does?). Social cohesion, moral guidance and entertainment are real effects of myths, but they are secondary and are also produced by customs, laws and art.

**Answer: A.**
themes: myth and the origin of philosophy

choix.texte: Provides answers to fundamental questions about their existence.
Gives guidance on how to live.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The major concern of the early Greek thinkers was on :

*Options as printed:* A) The basic substance out of which the universe is made up of.   B) The basic nature of things.   C) The origin of the universe.   D) The immutable root from which all things come.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The first Greek thinkers (Thales, Anaximander, Anaximenes and the other Ionian "physicists") asked what the universe is made of and where it comes from. Their answer took the form of a search for the *arche*, the primary stuff or first principle: water for Thales, the *apeiron* (the unlimited) for Anaximander, air for Anaximenes. The most standard formulation of their concern is therefore the **basic substance out of which the universe is made**.

Caution: options B, C and D describe closely related aspects of the same quest (the nature of things, the origin of the universe, the permanent root of change), so the printed question does not single out one of them unambiguously; it is left open for self-assessment.

**Intended answer: A (The basic substance out of which the universe is made up of).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: The first philosopher to explicitly formulate the question of being is :
questions.corrige_markdown:
Parmenides of Elea is credited with the first explicit formulation of the question of Being: his poem opposes the way of truth ("what is, is, and cannot not-be") to the way of opinion, and treats Being as one, ungenerated and unchanging. Heraclitus stressed becoming and flux, Anaxagoras explained the world by a mixture of seeds ordered by Mind (*nous*), and Aristotle, who came much later, made the study of "being as being" the object of first philosophy but did not formulate the question first.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Pythagoras' assertion that : ' knowledge is neither universal nor objective', can best be qualified as :

*Options as printed:* A) Subjectivism.   B) Scepticism.   C) Relativism.   D) Agnosticism.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The assertion that knowledge is neither universal nor objective is the position of the Sophists, summed up in the dictum of Protagoras that "man is the measure of all things" (the printed name "Pythagoras" is almost certainly a slip for Protagoras, since Pythagoras defended number as the principle of reality). If what is true or known depends on the person (or the culture) that perceives it, there is no single truth valid for everybody: this is **relativism**. Scepticism doubts that knowledge is possible, and agnosticism suspends judgement on whether (usually) God can be known; neither says that knowledge varies with the knower.

Caution: subjectivism (option A) is also a defensible name for the position (knowledge depends on the subject), and the printed name is wrong, so the question is left open for self-assessment.

**Intended answer: C (Relativism).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: Socratic Ethics is considered eudemonistic because :
questions.corrige_markdown:
A moral theory is *eudemonistic* (from the Greek *eudaimonia*, happiness or well-being) when it holds that the end of human action is happiness. For Socrates, virtue is knowledge and the virtuous life is the one that makes the soul good, and a good soul is the condition of a happy life: everyone seeks happiness, and virtue is the means by which it is attained. The label "eudemonistic" therefore refers to the aim of **attaining happiness**. Options B, C and D describe how virtue works (function, perfection of the soul) but not what makes the ethics eudemonistic.

**Answer: A.**

choix.texte: It is aimed at attaining happiness.
It is aimed at fulfilling its function of attaining one's virtue.
It is aimed at realizing one's functions.
It is aimed at making the soul perfect and good.

questions.enonce_markdown: The main characteristics of Plato's Forms are :
questions.corrige_markdown:
For Plato the Forms (Ideas) are the true, intelligible realities of which the objects of the senses are imperfect copies. They are grasped by the intellect, not by the senses, so they are **immaterial**; they do not change or decay, so they are **immutable**; and they exist outside time, so they are **eternal**. The sensible things that participate in them are the ones that are material and mutable.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: According to Aristotle, primary substances are made up of two elements, namely :
questions.corrige_markdown:
Aristotle's doctrine of *hylomorphism* (from *hyle*, matter, and *morphe*, form) holds that every individual (primary) substance, such as this man or this horse, is a compound of **matter** (what it is made of, the potentiality) and **form** (what makes it the kind of thing it is, the actuality). "Substance and accident" are two of the categories of being, not the constituents of a substance, and "essence and existence" is the distinction later developed by Aquinas.

**Answer: A.**
themes: aristotle and the categories of being

questions.enonce_markdown: St, Thomas Aquinas considers the relationship between Faith and Reason as being :
questions.corrige_markdown:
Aquinas holds that faith and reason have the same source, God, so truth cannot contradict truth: reason can establish the "preambles of faith" (for example that God exists) and faith gives access to truths that exceed reason (the mysteries, such as the Trinity). They are different in method but they work together and **complement each other**, so that revelation completes and perfects what natural reason can know. They are not opposed (option A), they are not identical (option D), and while they are distinct in their starting points (option C), the question asks about their relationship, which is complementarity.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The major objective of Descartes in methodic doubt was :
questions.corrige_markdown:
Descartes' methodic (methodical) doubt is a *method*, not a doctrine: he doubts every belief that can be doubted in order to find something absolutely certain, a firm foundation on which to rebuild knowledge (the *cogito*, "I think, therefore I am", is the first certainty reached). Doubting everything (option B) is the means, not the objective, and the doubt is not a sceptic's final position. Options C and D concern faith and God, which are not the aim of the method.

**Answer: A.**

choix.texte: To arrive at true and certain knowledge.
To doubt all his previous knowledge.

questions.enonce_markdown: The two forms of experience according to John Locke are :
questions.corrige_markdown:
Locke, the founder of British empiricism, rejects innate ideas: the mind at birth is like a blank sheet and all its ideas come from experience. Experience takes two forms: **sensation** (external experience, through the senses, giving ideas of colour, sound, hardness...) and **reflection** (internal experience, the mind's observation of its own operations such as thinking, doubting and willing). "Intuition and deduction" are Descartes' ways of reaching knowledge, and "matter and form" are Aristotelian principles.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The Empericists claim knowledge is only attainable through :
questions.corrige_markdown:
Empiricism (Locke, Berkeley, Hume) is the theory that all knowledge originates in and is justified by **experience**, mainly sense experience. Reason as the source of knowledge independent of experience is the claim of the rationalists (Descartes, Spinoza, Leibniz). Faith and dogma are not sources of knowledge for the empiricists.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: By describing the African mind as being 'pre-logical' Levy Bruhl meant :
questions.corrige_markdown:
The French ethnologist Lucien Levy-Bruhl described what he called the "primitive" or "pre-logical" mentality as one that is not governed by the laws of thought of Western logic, in particular the principle of non-contradiction: it is guided by mystical participation between beings and is indifferent to contradiction. The claim is that this mind **does not respect the laws of thought** (it is not that it lacks any thinking). Options B and C draw conclusions Levy-Bruhl did not state in these terms, and option D is not what "pre-logical" means. African philosophers (Towa, Hountondji, Wiredu) reject the thesis as a colonial prejudice.

**Answer: A.**

choix.texte: The African mind does not respect the Laws of thought.
The Africans are not thinking beings.
The Africans are attached to their cultures

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following justifies Hegel's thesis on History and the Africans?
questions.corrige_markdown:
In his Lectures on the Philosophy of History, Hegel presents history as the progress of the Spirit towards consciousness of freedom, and he places Africa outside this movement: Africa is described as "unhistorical", a continent without development of its own, still at the stage of undeveloped Spirit. His thesis on History and the Africans is therefore that the **Africans are ahistorical**, which he then used to justify their exclusion from the history of civilisation. The other options (inability to philosophise, irrationality, lack of freedom) are consequences that racist readings drew, not the formulation of the thesis on history. The thesis is rejected by African thinkers as a prejudice with no factual basis.

**Answer: B.**

choix.texte: The Africans are not free people

questions.enonce_markdown: An outstanding Cameroonian proponent of Ethnophilosophy is :
questions.corrige_markdown:
Ethnophilosophy is the trend that presents the collective world view, beliefs and wisdom of African peoples as a philosophy (Tempels is its founder). In the Cameroonian syllabus, **Basile Fouda** is classed among its proponents. Marcien Towa, Fabien Eboussi Boulaga and Njoh Mouelle are on the other side: they belong to the professional (critical) trend and criticised ethnophilosophy as a collective, uncritical and static discourse, so they cannot be the answer. Note: the classification of Fouda follows the course notes; other authors may classify him differently.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
An outstanding Cameroonian proponent of Professional Philosophy is :

*Options as printed:* A) Meinrad Hebga.   B) Njoh Mouelle.   C) Basile Fouda.   D) Marcien Towa.
questions.corrige_markdown:
Professional philosophy is the trend that holds that philosophy is a critical, rational and individual discipline, not the collective world view of a people, and that it must be done with the rigour of the discipline as practised everywhere. In Cameroon its best-known representatives are **Marcien Towa**, who criticised ethnophilosophy and called for a philosophy that frees Africa through critical rationality, and **Njoh Mouelle**, who developed a philosophy of change and of the human person. Both are classed as professional philosophers, so the printed question has two defensible answers (B and D); it is left open for self-assessment. In the course notes Hebga and Fouda are placed on the traditionalist or ethnophilosophical side.

**Intended answer: D (Marcien Towa).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: The book 'Bantu Philosophy' was written by :
questions.corrige_markdown:
"Bantu Philosophy" is the work of the Belgian Franciscan missionary **Placide Tempels**, who worked among the Luba of the Congo and published it in the 1940s. In it he argues that the Bantu conception of being is that of vital force, which made him the founder of ethnophilosophy. Oruka is the author of the concept of sage philosophy, Hountondji and Wiredu are critical professional philosophers.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Who among these are the major proponents of Ethnophilosophy ?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Option A is the only one that names ethnophilosophers: the printed names "Pacid Tempels" and "Basile Tempels" are misprints for **Placide Tempels** (founder of the trend with *Bantu Philosophy*) and **Basile Fouda** (the Cameroonian proponent, see question 27). Towa and Eboussi Boulaga (option B) are critics of ethnophilosophy and belong to the professional trend; Hountondji (option C) is the best-known critic of ethnophilosophy; Nkrumah (option D) belongs to the nationalistic-ideological trend and Oruka to sage philosophy.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Which amongst these is the most suitable objective of the nationalistic ideological school of African Philosophy ?

*Options as printed:* A) Promote African unity.   B) Enhance African personality.   C) Militate for the liberation of the Africans.   D) Seek solutions for the development of the African.
questions.corrige_markdown:
Odera Oruka's classification distinguishes four trends in contemporary African philosophy: ethnophilosophy, philosophic sagacity, the nationalistic-ideological trend and professional philosophy. The nationalistic-ideological trend is the thought of the leaders of the independence movements (Nkrumah, Nyerere, Senghor and others), whose first aim was the political and cultural **liberation** of Africans from colonial domination and the building of a free society. That is why the objective best linked to the label "nationalistic" is liberation.

Caution: unity, African personality and development are also goals of that same trend, so several options are defensible; the question is left open for self-assessment.

**Intended answer: C (Militate for the liberation of the Africans).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: The concept 'Sage Philosophy' was coined by :
questions.corrige_markdown:
"Sage philosophy" is the concept of the Kenyan philosopher **Henry Odera Oruka**, who recorded the critical, individual reflections of wise men and women in traditional communities (the sages) to show that traditional Africa had individual philosophical thought, not only a collective world view. Tempels is the founder of ethnophilosophy, Hountondji a critic of it and Gyekye a Ghanaian philosopher of the Akan tradition and of communitarianism.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The study of reality existing in everything and in every Being in the African universe best describes :
questions.corrige_markdown:
Metaphysics is the branch of philosophy that studies reality as such, being and what exists in everything (its nature, its first principles). When this study is applied to the African conception of the universe, in which every being is understood as carrying a vital force, it is **African metaphysics**. Ethics studies conduct, epistemology knowledge and religion is a system of beliefs and worship, not a study of reality as such.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which among the following is the most appropriate 'Order of Being' in the African universe in the ascending order?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The African world view arranges reality in a hierarchy of levels of being, from the lowest to the highest: the level of the **laws of nature** (the physical world: minerals, plants, animals), then the **moral** level (human beings and the moral order of the community), then the **religious** level (ancestors, spirits, divinities) and finally the **metaphysical** level (the Supreme Being, source of all forces). In ascending order the sequence is therefore: laws of nature, moral, religious, metaphysical. Option A gives the same four levels in the descending order, and options C and D scramble them.

**Answer: B.**

choix.texte: Metaphysical, Religious, Moral and Laws of nature.
Laws of nature, Moral, Religious and Metaphysical.
Religious, Metaphysical, Moral and Laws of nature.
Metaphysical, Laws of nature, Moral and Religious.

questions.enonce_markdown: The supernatural forces which defy any scientific explanation which can be, manipulated by man for both good and evil purposes can be qualified as :
questions.corrige_markdown:
The description has three elements: forces that are supernatural, that defy scientific explanation, and that people can manipulate **for good as well as for evil**. This is **mysticism** (the mystical power of African traditional thought, which can be used beneficially, as in healing and protection, or harmfully). Witchcraft (option C) is only one harmful use of such powers and is by definition directed at evil; rationality and epistemology are not forces at all.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The main distinction between African indigenous democracy and Western Liberal democracy is :
questions.corrige_markdown:
The African philosophers who studied traditional political systems (Wiredu, Gyekye and others) stress that in indigenous African democracy decisions are reached by discussion until **consensus** is obtained, so that no one is left in a defeated minority, whereas Western liberal democracy decides by **majority rule** after a vote among competing parties. Options B and C do not describe the contrast (indigenous democracy is not simply hereditary elitism, and the issue is not only the number of parties). Option D (communitarian against representative) names an attached feature but not the main procedural distinction.

**Answer: A.**

choix.texte: Rule by consensus and majority rule

questions.enonce_markdown: The view that people are always motivated by self-interest and cannot be expected to act otherwise is known as ?
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Psychological egoism** is a *descriptive* theory about human nature: every human action is, in fact, motivated by self-interest, so people cannot act otherwise. **Ethical egoism** (option A) is a *normative* theory: people ought to act in their own interest, which presupposes that they could act otherwise. "Accidental egoism" and "Freudian egoism" are not standard names of positions in ethics.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: According to the pro-life argument, the moral permissibility of an act is based on :
questions.corrige_markdown:
The pro-life position (for example in the abortion debate) holds that human life is sacred and has intrinsic value from its beginning, so that an act is morally permissible only if it respects the **sanctity of life**. Individual or human freedom (options A and D) is the basis of the pro-choice argument, and social laws (option B) are not what the pro-life argument bases morality on.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following pairs are both acts for which man can be held fully responsible on the one hand and not fully responsible on the other hand ?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Moral responsibility requires knowledge and free consent: acts that are voluntary and deliberate make the agent fully responsible, while acts that are involuntary or accidental do not. A deliberate **abortion** and a deliberate **homicide** are voluntary acts of the agent, so he is fully responsible for them. A **miscarriage** (a spontaneous loss of pregnancy) and an accidental **drowning** are not chosen by the person, who is therefore not fully responsible. The first pair of option D is the one for full responsibility and the second pair the one for partial responsibility; option B reverses them and options A and C mix voluntary and involuntary acts within a pair.

**Answer: D.**

choix.texte: Homicide and Miscarriage, Abortion and Drowning.
Miscarriage and drowning, Abortion and Homicide.
Abortion and Miscarriage, Homicide and Drowning.
Abortion and Homicide, Miscarriage and Drowning.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Which moral principle adequately describes a lady who indulges herself into prostitution in order to alleviate poverty in her family ?

*Options as printed:* A) Double effect.   B) Higher good.   C) Utilitarianism.   D) Personalism.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The woman acts in a situation of conflict between two values: her own dignity and the avoidance of an act that is generally considered wrong on the one hand, and the survival and well-being of her family on the other. Reasoning by the **principle of the higher good** means choosing, among conflicting values, the one that is considered higher; she subordinates one value to the survival of her family. This is the principle that best describes the stated motive. The principle of double effect applies to an act that has a good and a bad effect and requires that the act itself be morally acceptable and that the bad effect not be the means to the good one, which does not fit here since the act is itself the means. Utilitarianism judges acts by their consequences for the greatest number, and personalism by respect for the dignity of the person.

Caution: depending on the course notes, options A and C can also be defended, so the question is left open for self-assessment.

**Intended answer: B (Higher good).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown:
When J.J. Rousseau declares that « Man is born free, but everywhere is in chains » he means that :

*Options as printed:* A) The other is a limitation to man's freedom.   B) The society is a hindrance to man's growth.   C) The alienable rights are limited.   D) The inalienable rights are limited.
questions.corrige_markdown:
For Rousseau man in the state of nature is free and good, but the societies that have actually developed (with property, inequality and unjust laws) have placed him under constraints, so that he lives everywhere in dependence. The sentence is the opening of the *Social Contract*, where he looks for a legitimate form of association that would restore freedom. In the reading closest to the text, **society as it exists limits and hinders man's natural freedom** (option B). Option A is the thesis of Sartre's existentialism rather than of Rousseau. Options C and D concern rights that are limited; Rousseau does hold that freedom is inalienable, so that D is not wrong as a statement, but it does not express what the sentence means.

Caution: B and D are both defensible readings of the printed sentence, so the question is left open for self-assessment.

**Intended answer: B (The society is a hindrance to man's growth).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: In 'The Republic', Plato posits that the culminating virtue found in the state is :
questions.corrige_markdown:
In the *Republic* Plato describes the ideal state as made of three classes: the rulers (guardians), whose virtue is **wisdom**; the auxiliaries (soldiers), whose virtue is **courage**; and the producers, with **temperance** (harmony) shared by all. When each class does its own work and does not interfere with the others, the state is **just**: justice is the virtue that includes the other three and completes them, the culminating virtue of the state.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which amongst the system of government is ruled by a select few ?
questions.corrige_markdown:
In the classical classification of forms of government (Plato, Aristotle), the rule of a SELECT few, understood as the best, is **aristocracy** (from the Greek *aristos*, best). Plutocracy is the rule of the wealthy, timocracy the rule of those who love honour (or hold property) and tyranny the rule of one man who has taken power by force.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Nietzsche's description of the state as a ' cold monsters' best validates :

*Options as printed:* A) The use of war by the state.   B) The use of violence by the state.   C) The use of power by the state.   D) The misuse of power by the state:
questions.corrige_markdown:
In *Thus Spoke Zarathustra* Nietzsche calls the state the coldest of all cold monsters: an impersonal power that claims to be the people while it destroys the creative life of individuals and imposes itself on them. The image describes the state as an impersonal and oppressive machine whose power rests on coercion, so the description is best linked to the **use of violence by the state** (its coercive power over individuals).

Caution: war, power and the misuse of power can also be linked with the image, so the printed question does not identify one reading unambiguously; it is left open for self-assessment.

**Intended answer: B (The use of violence by the state).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: The conception of God as the creator of the universe but who is far removed from it is best described as :
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Deism** holds that God exists and created the universe but then withdrew from it: He does not intervene in its course or in human affairs (the image of the clockmaker). Theism affirms a God who is both creator and involved in the world (providence, revelation), atheism denies the existence of God and agnosticism claims that His existence cannot be known.

**Answer: B.**
themes: arguments for the existence of god

questions.enonce_markdown: Aquinas' knowledge of God by Analogy is represented aptly in the following sequence :
questions.corrige_markdown:
Aquinas asks how human words can be used of God and examines three modes of predication in turn. **Univocal** predication (the same meaning for God and creatures) is rejected, because it would reduce God to the level of creatures. **Equivocal** predication (completely different meanings) is rejected as well, because then we could say nothing true of God. The solution is **analogical** predication: words such as "good" or "wise" apply to God and to creatures in meanings that are partly the same and partly different, on the ground that creatures resemble their cause. The sequence in which the argument unfolds is therefore: univocal, equivocal, analogical.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A situation in which innocent children are killed by unidenfied men can best be described as :
questions.corrige_markdown:
In the discussion of the problem of evil, **moral evil** is the evil that results from the free choices of human beings (murder, cruelty, injustice). Killing innocent children by men is an evil caused by human wrongdoing. Natural (physical) evil is the suffering caused by nature without human agency (earthquake, disease) and metaphysical evil is the imperfection and finitude of created beings.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The Sartrean assertion that « Existence precedes essence » can best be interpreted as :
questions.corrige_markdown:
For Sartre, a manufactured object (a paper-knife) has an essence, its definition and purpose, before it exists, since the craftsman conceives it first. Human beings are not made according to a concept: they first exist, find themselves in the world, and only afterwards define what they are through their free choices and actions. "Existence precedes essence" therefore means that **there is no pre-given, defined human nature**, and that man is what he makes of himself. Options C and D (determinism and predestination) say the opposite, and option B affirms a fixed nature.

**Answer: A.**

choix.texte: There is no defined human nature.
There is a defined human nature.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Philosophy and Religion both seek the truth but from different angles precisely in that :

*Options as printed:* A) Philosophy deliberates on reason while Religion harps on revelation.   B) Philosophy is objective while Religion is subjective.   C) Philosophy is reason bound while Religion is faith bound.   D) Philosophy is sometimes dogmatic while Religion is never dogmatic.
questions.corrige_markdown:
Philosophy and religion both ask about the origin and meaning of the world and of human life, but they proceed differently: philosophy relies on **reason** (argument, criticism, evidence open to every inquirer), while religion rests on **faith** in a revealed truth. Options B and D are wrong (religion is not simply subjective, and religion is dogmatic by nature).

Caution: options A and C express practically the same contrast (reason against revelation, reason against faith), so the printed question has two defensible answers; it is left open for self-assessment.

**Intended answer: C (Philosophy is reason bound while Religion is faith bound).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown:
One of the outstanding usefulness of Philosophy to humanity at large is that :

*Options as printed:* A) It liberates the human mind from cultural precepts.   B) It enhances the human world view.   C) It distorts the spirit of creativity.   D) It sharpens the human thinking capacity.
questions.corrige_markdown:
Philosophy trains critical and analytical thinking: it teaches how to define terms, build and test arguments and detect fallacies, which sharpens the **thinking capacity** of every person whatever the field. Option C is false (philosophy stimulates creativity). Options A and B (freeing the mind from prejudice, widening one's world view) are genuine benefits too, and they follow from the sharpening of critical thinking.

Caution: A, B and D are all acceptable benefits of philosophy and the question says only "one of" them, so the printed question has no single best answer; it is left open for self-assessment.

**Intended answer: D (It sharpens the human thinking capacity).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.
